Koh Samui has three waterfalls worth the drive. Na Muang 1 is free, about 18 m high and has a swimmable pool 5–10 minutes from the car park. Na Muang 2, 1 km further up the same hillside, is a steep 20–40 minute climb with fixed ropes to a series of tiers about 80 m high in total. Hin Lad, 2–3 km inland from Nathon, is a forest walk of about two hours return. All three run fullest October–January and thin to a trickle February–April; parking at Na Muang costs about 20 THB for a scooter and 60 THB for a car.

This hub compares every fall, gives the opening hours and fees we could confirm for late 2026, shows when there is water, and ends with a one-day route that pairs the waterfalls with the island's best inland temples and viewpoints. Each waterfall also has its own detailed page: Na Muang Waterfalls 1 and 2, the Na Muang 2 climb and Hin Lad Waterfall.

Map of the waterfalls and viewpoints

All of Samui's waterfalls are on the island's forested central ridge, which climbs to 635 m at Khao Pom. Na Muang 1 and 2 sit in Na Mueang subdistrict in the south-centre, a short drive inland from Route 4169, the ring road. Hin Lad is on the western slope above Nathon, on the opposite side of the ridge. The map below shows the falls; the table under it gives the coordinates of the waterfalls plus the temples and viewpoints we pair them with.

Koh Samui waterfalls compared

If you only have time for one, choose by what you want to do. Na Muang 1 is the swim. Na Muang 2 is the workout and the biggest drop. Hin Lad is the quiet forest walk with a temple at the start. None of them charges an official entry fee; the costs are parking and, at Na Muang 2, a possible small charge on private land.

WaterfallAreaWalkFeeSwimBest for
Na Muang 1Na Mueang, south-centre5–10 min, flat, shadedFree; parking ~20 THB scooter / ~60 THB carYes: wide pool under an ~18 m drop; deepens suddenlyFamilies, a quick swim, tour groups
Na Muang 2Na Mueang, 1 km further up20–40 min each way, steep, fixed ropesLeft-hand path signed as a free walk; some visitors report ~50 THB on a private routeSmall plunge pools on the tiers; very slippery rockFit walkers with grippy shoes
Hin LadAng Thong subdistrict, 2–3 km from Nathon30–45 min between tiers; ~2 h returnNo published fee (donation box reported)Small pools; refreshing, not for lapsA quiet forest walk on the west side

Good to know: Samui's waterfalls are small by mainland standards. Visit them for a cool swim and a forest walk in the wet months, not for Niagara. From February to April expect thin ribbons of water over dark rock.

Na Muang 1: the easy swim

Na Muang 1 (9.4668, 99.9838) is the island's best-known waterfall and the only one most visitors see. From the car park a shaded path of 5–10 minutes passes food stalls, a café and a souvenir shop before reaching an amphitheatre of purple-grey rock and a single drop of about 18 m into a wide pool. The listed hours are 09:00–17:00 daily (one listing says from 08:00); entry is free.

  • Swimming: the pool is big enough for a proper swim and children often jump in from low rocks at the edge. The depth changes without warning, so check before you jump and keep small children within arm's reach.
  • Facilities: toilets, cold drinks, snacks and souvenir stalls by the car park. Souvenir sellers in the car park can be pushy; a smile and "mai ao, khop khun" (no thanks) works.
  • Crowds: tour minibuses from Chaweng and Lamai arrive from about 10:00 and the pool is busiest 10:00–14:00. Arrive at 09:00 and you will often share it with only a handful of people.
  • Time needed: 45 minutes to 1.5 hours with a swim.

Full details, including the step-by-step walk and a month-by-month flow table, are on our Na Muang Waterfall guide.

Na Muang 2: the climb

Na Muang 2 (9.4723, 99.9905) is a chain of at least five tiers dropping about 80 m in total, the tallest waterfall on Samui. It is open 09:00–18:00. Most people drive up the hill road past Na Muang 1 to the car parks at the top end, take the left-hand jungle path (signed as a free jungle walk) about 100 m downhill past a small shop, cross a wooden bridge and then climb. If you are not crossing a wooden bridge at the start, you are on the wrong path. The right-hand route leads through a private café and garden with coloured water slides; reviewers rate its views lower and swimming at the top is not allowed there.

The climb takes 20–40 minutes each way depending on fitness and how wet the rock is. Expect tree roots, mud, boulder steps and several sections with fixed ropes. The site fills by about 10:30, so start early. Our full route and safety notes are on the Na Muang 2 page.

Footwear and ropes

  • Wear closed shoes with a lugged sole: trail runners, approach shoes or sports sandals with heel straps. Flip-flops are how most injuries start.
  • Test each rope before you load it, keep three points of contact, and go one person at a time on rope sections.
  • Keep both hands free: carry water and your phone in a small backpack, not in your hands.
  • Do not climb above the marked tiers for photos. The fatal falls here happened on the upper tiers, mostly to people stepping back for a picture.

Hin Lad and the forest temple

Hin Lad (9.5205, 99.9556) is on the west side of the island, about 2–3 km inland from Nathon in Ang Thong subdistrict. The trail starts beside a forest temple, usually called Wat Namtok Hin Lad (the Hin Lad Waterfall Temple), and climbs a stream valley past several small tiers and pools. Reaching the first tier is quick; the walk between tiers takes 30–45 minutes on steep, uneven ground with roots and rocks, so allow about two hours for the full walk and a swim.

  • Fee and hours: no official fee or opening hours are published. One listing gives 08:00–17:00 and visitors report a donation box; go in daylight and bring small notes.
  • Parking: visitors report space for cars and scooters near the trailhead, reached on a good road.
  • Swimming: the pools are small and cool, good for a dip after the climb.
  • Temple etiquette: the trail passes an active monastery. Cover shoulders and knees near the buildings and keep voices low.

Read the full Hin Lad Waterfall guide before you go, and combine it with lunch or the evening market in Nathon.

Smaller falls and jungle pools

You will see other "waterfalls" advertised on Samui, often as part of a zipline, ATV or jungle tour. Some are small seasonal streams on private land; some are man-made pools. We list only falls we can describe accurately, so this guide covers the three above and does not name falls we have not been able to confirm for 2026.

  • The 2-hour ATV rides in the hills include a short walk to a stream fall; see ATV and quad bike tours.
  • A zipline park in the Maenam hills includes a short waterfall walk after the ride; see zipline tours.
  • The Secret Buddha Garden has a small stream with little cascades running through the sculptures.

Outside the October–January rains, most of these smaller falls are dry or close to it.

When the waterfalls have water

Samui's rain pattern is the opposite of Phuket's. The north-east monsoon brings most rain from October to December, peaking in November, and that is when the falls run hardest. February to April is the driest stretch: lovely for the beach, poor for waterfalls. The table uses long-term averages for the Ko Samui weather station (1991–2020).

March1165Low; a storm can refresh the falls for a day or two.
April836Lowest flow, hottest month (highs ~32 °C). Expect a trickle.

Fees, hours and parking

None of the three waterfalls has an official ticket office. The fees you will meet are parking and, occasionally, a small charge from landowners on alternative paths. Carry 20, 50 and 100 THB notes.

At Na Muang, use the waterfall's own car park, not the first lot by the elephant camp on the way in, even if a sign or attendant waves you towards it.

How to get there

The waterfalls are inland, off the tourist strip, and public transport does not serve them. Your options are a scooter or car, a taxi with waiting time, or a tour.

FromTo Na Muang 1 (approx.)To Hin Lad (approx.)
Lamai11 km, 15–20 min via Hua Thanon and Route 416922 km, 30–35 min
Chaweng20 km, 30–40 min via Lamai27 km, 40–50 min
Nathon12 km, 15–20 min south on Route 41693 km, 5–10 min
Bophut / Maenam22–25 km, 35–45 min13–18 km, 20–30 min via Nathon
Airport23 km, 35–45 min25 km, 40 min
  • Scooter: the roads to Na Muang 1 and Hin Lad are paved and fine for a 125 cc scooter. The hill road up to Na Muang 2 is steep: ride in low gear, brake before bends, not in them. You need your licence plus an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category, and a helmet (fines up to 2,000 THB per person since June 2025). See motorbike rental and Koh Samui roads.
  • Car: the easiest choice for families; compact cars cost about 800–1,200 THB a day. See car rental.
  • Taxi or Grab: taxis are unmetered, so agree a return fare with waiting time before you leave. Grab will get you there from Chaweng or Lamai, but finding one back from the waterfalls is hit-and-miss. A full-day taxi costs about 2,000–3,000 THB and makes sense if you follow the day plan below.
  • Songthaew: don't rely on them. There is no regular service to the falls and they stop running by 20:00–22:00. More in getting around Koh Samui.

A waterfall and temple day plan

This route links the falls with the inland south-east sights in one loop, with the hottest hours spent in the shade or in the water. It works best by car with a driver or on a 4x4 jungle safari, because the Secret Buddha Garden road is too steep for most scooter riders.

  1. 09:00 Na Muang 1: swim before the tour groups arrive.
  2. 10:00 Drive up to Na Muang 2 and climb the left-hand path (allow 1.5–2 h with a rest at the top).
  3. 12:15 Lunch at a local restaurant on Route 4169 in Na Mueang.
  4. 13:30 Wat Khunaram, home of the mummified monk Luang Pho Daeng (20–30 min; cover shoulders and knees).
  5. 14:15 Secret Buddha Garden by 4x4: sculptures, a stream and the coolest air on the island (45–60 min; 100 THB in recent reports).
  6. 16:00 The Red Temple (Wat Sila Ngu) or the Overlap Stone viewpoint above Maret.
  7. 17:00 Hin Ta and Hin Yai at the south end of Lamai, then dinner in Lamai.

Prefer the west side? Pair Hin Lad in the morning with lunch in Nathon and a sunset at Lipa Noi or Taling Ngam; see Koh Samui sunset spots.

Jungle tours that include waterfalls

If you don't want to drive, a tour is the simplest way to see the falls and the hill sights in one day.

  • 4x4 jungle safari: the standard market tour runs about 7 hours (roughly 10:00–17:00) and costs around 1,700 THB in 2026. It usually includes Hin Ta and Hin Yai, a swim at Na Muang, Wat Khunaram, the Secret Buddha Garden, a hilltop Thai lunch and the Big Buddha, with entry fees and lunch included. Ask us for a shared or private safari on our jungle safari page.
  • ATV and quad: 1–2 hour guided rides on hill tracks from about 1,490 THB per rider; the longer rides add a stream fall. See ATV tours.
  • Zipline: a 1-hour canopy course with a short waterfall walk; see zipline.

Elephant camps near Na Muang: our view

The road to Na Muang is lined with animal attractions, and this is where many visitors end up doing something they later regret. Visitor reports from 2026 describe elephants kept in cramped enclosures near the Na Muang car parks, with rides still bookable at some of them. The old Namuang Safari Park address now trades as Samui Elephant Kingdom, which says it no longer offers riding; older listings still describe rides and animal shows, and we have not been able to confirm the current set-up.

Our position is simple: we don't recommend any elephant riding, chained-elephant feeding or animal shows on Samui. If you want to see elephants, choose a no-riding, no-bathing sanctuary; our Koh Samui elephant sanctuary guide explains how to tell the difference. Practical tip: drive past the first car park by the elephant camp and park at the waterfall's own car park.

Safety at the waterfalls

Samui's waterfalls look gentle but have a serious record. At least four foreign visitors have died in falls at Na Muang 2 since 2019, most recently a 22-year-old French tourist on 5 January 2026 who slipped on the fifth tier while taking photos. An Indian visitor died there in November 2024 after climbing a cliff for a view despite a warning sign, and an Italian (June 2024) and a British visitor (May 2025) were seriously injured. A rescue from the upper tiers takes hours.

  • Slippery rock: wet granite and algae are as slick as ice. Stay off the lip of any drop and never step backwards for a photo.
  • Flash floods: after heavy rain, especially October–December, water levels can rise within minutes and the colour turns brown. Get out of the stream bed if the water rises or clouds over the hills turn black.
  • No jumping: pool depths change with the season and hidden rocks are common. Jump only where you have checked the depth yourself, and not at all at Na Muang 2.
  • Mosquitoes and dengue: dengue is present in Thailand all year and peaks in the rainy season. Use a DEET or picaridin repellent and cover up in the forest.
  • Valuables: don't leave bags on the rocks while you swim. Lock the scooter seat, take the key and leave passports at the hotel.
  • Emergency: ambulance 1669, Tourist Police 1155. Mobile signal is patchy on the upper trails. Check that your travel insurance covers hiking and scooter riding: one injured visitor's hospital bill exceeded 4.4 million THB.

What to bring

  • Closed shoes or strapped sports sandals with grip
  • 1–2 litres of water per person
  • Swimwear and a quick-dry towel
  • Insect repellent and sunscreen
  • A small backpack and a waterproof phone pouch
  • Cash in small notes for parking and drinks
  • A sarong or light layer to cover shoulders and knees for the temples

More safety advice for the island is on our safety and precautions page and the hospitals guide.

Waterfalls with children

Na Muang 1 is the family waterfall: a flat, shaded 5–10 minute walk, toilets and snacks by the car park, and shallow edges to the pool where small children can paddle while older ones swim. Keep toddlers within arm's reach, because the bottom shelves quickly. Na Muang 2 and the upper part of Hin Lad are not suitable for young children; fit teenagers can manage Na Muang 2 in dry weather with close supervision. Pack spare clothes, a towel and repellent, and go early to avoid the midday heat. More ideas: Koh Samui with kids.

Leave no trace

The pools are drinking and washing water for farms and temples downstream. Don't use soap or shampoo in the water, take every bottle and wrapper back to the car park, and don't carve or paint on the rocks. At Hin Lad, the trail passes through temple land: keep music off and voices low.

A rainy-day plan

If heavy rain sets in, the waterfalls are still one of the better things to do on Samui, but change the plan. Swim at Na Muang 1 only if the water is clear, skip the climbs at Na Muang 2 and Hin Lad, and spend the rest of the day at Wat Khunaram, the temples or a cooking class. Look again the next morning: after a dry night the flow is strong and the trails start to drain.

Waterfalls in the morning, the sea in the afternoon

A waterfall morning leaves the afternoon free for the water. The Pig Island Sunset Tour (1,550 THB adult, 1,350 THB child 3–11, 5–6 hours with dinner) runs in the afternoon and evening from Thong Krut on the south-west coast, 15–20 minutes from Na Muang. For a full day at sea another time, the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult, 1,250 THB child) runs every day of the year. Hotel transfers are included from the main areas; remote areas pay a surcharge, which we confirm when you book.

Ang Thong National Marine Park is closed from 1 November to 15 December every year; our Ang Thong speedboat day tour (1,800 THB adult) restarts on 16 December 2026.
